crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: AI and Authorship
children.blurb: AI and authorship covers the questions of who or what counts as an author when a model contributes to a text, an image, a dataset or a piece of code, and how credit, accountability and originality are assigned in that arrangement.

children.name: Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking
children.blurb: Fabricated citations are references that look plausible but point to papers, authors, journals or DOIs that do not exist, or that misattribute real work to the wrong source.

children.name: Training Data and Academic Work
children.blurb: Training data in academic work covers the corpora, datasets and text collections that machine learning models learn from, together with the scholarly record those collections are drawn from.

children.name: Ethics Review with AI Assistance
children.blurb: Ethics review with AI assistance covers the use of machine learning tools inside institutional review boards, research ethics committees, and similar bodies that assess human subjects research, animal work, and dual use concerns.

children.name: Provenance of Research Images and Data
children.blurb: Provenance of research images and data covers the record of where a figure, dataset, or measurement came from, who handled it, and what was done to it before publication.

sections.body: This section covers the rules and practices that keep AI assisted research honest, from who counts as an author to whether a cited paper exists at all. In practice, AI is now used to draft manuscripts, suggest citations, screen ethics applications and generate or edit figures, and each of those uses creates a paper trail that has to be checked. Authorship is the clearest case, since journals generally require authors to take responsibility for a paper, which a model cannot do. Fact checking has become a routine step because language models produce plausible citations that do not exist. Training data provenance matters because models are built from published work, and researchers increasingly need to know what went in. Image and data provenance covers the detection of manipulated figures and the documentation of where a dataset came from.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts of this are settled. Fabricated citations are easy to catch with a search, and most publishers now require disclosure of AI use in writing and review. Ethics review with AI assistance is more contested, since a model can triage applications but cannot judge risk or consent. Training data provenance remains largely unsolved, because most large models do not disclose their sources in a way that supports citation or compensation. Image provenance has improved through screening tools, but detection still fails on well made manipulations and on images that were never published. The honest limit across the whole section is that verification depends on human labour, and the volume of AI assisted submissions is rising faster than the capacity to check them.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages here split into the two ends of a paper, what goes in and what comes out. AI and Authorship deals with credit and responsibility, and it is the place to start if you are working out who is accountable for a model assisted draft. Fabricated Citations and Fact Checking sits next to it, covering the verification step that catches references a model invented. Training Data and Academic Work looks upstream at the published literature that models are built from, which is where questions of consent and attribution begin. Ethics Review with AI Assistance covers the institutional process, including where a model can help and where a committee still has to decide. Provenance of Research Images and Data closes the loop on the output side, covering how figures and datasets are documented and checked. Read together they describe a single chain from source material to published claim, and each page covers one link where that chain tends to break.
